seasons.seasonNote:
Fred Beresford’s Warriors finished 9–0–2, described at the time as the school’s first unbeaten football team. The early schedule notice recorded a scrimmage with Lynn Classical at Stackpole Field, where tackle March and end O’Neil drew attention. After a 7–7 opening tie with Swampscott, Saugus won six straight. The Daily Evening Item described a light team that used a shift to set up its end runs. The postseason recap reports that only about 30 candidates turned out and that injuries exposed the lack of experienced reserves. The Item put the team’s average weight at 142 pounds and described Pike as a runner, passer and drop-kicker in Beresford’s open offense.

Danvers visited on October 7 for the home opener. An October 24 report said the Danvers coach withdrew his team with Saugus leading 7–0. The referee awarded Saugus a 1–0 forfeit, which Beresford declined to accept. The 11-game postseason table uses 1–0, while two other newspaper roundups list the 7–0 score on the field.

At Methuen’s Pelham Street Playstead on October 12, fullback Franklin “Ooze” Pike scored both Saugus touchdowns in a 14–7 win, opening the scoring on a 65-yard first-quarter run. Captain Edward “Googie” Amery added both extra points. On October 21, with about a minute left in a scoreless home game against Wellesley, Amery broke a 95-yard run and Pike carried the ball over for a 6–0 win.

Saugus shut out Somersworth, New Hampshire, 32–0. On November 18 it held a much larger Coburn Classical Institute team from Waterville, Maine, to a 0–0 tie before a reported 7,000 spectators at Stackpole Field. The game report highlighted the punting, and the Globe grouped Saugus with Winchester and Norwood among Greater Boston’s standout small-school teams. Albert J. Woodlock also named Saugus among teams unbeaten against Massachusetts opponents. The postseason account reports that Coburn had also tied Colby’s second team, beaten Maine’s second team and lost narrowly to the Dartmouth freshmen.

The year-end score table records a 52–7 win over Braintree and a 24–6 victory at Danvers on Thanksgiving, November 30. The latter was played in the mud two days before the finale. The November rematch followed the October forfeit.

On December 2, Saugus beat Woburn 20–9 at Stackpole Field before nearly 2,000 spectators. John O’Neil recovered a punt touched by Woburn, and a pass from Kenerson to Pool helped set up Amery’s opening touchdown. Pike scored on fourth down on the next Saugus scoring drive, and Amery kicked the extra point. Pike later broke a 60-yard run before being tackled, sprained his ankle and briefly left the game. Amery intercepted a pass and returned it to midfield before halftime. Woburn closed to 13–9, then Pike scored again in the fourth quarter and Amery kicked his second extra point. Kenerson was injured on a late passing play and left the game.

The December recap lists O’Neil and George Nicholson at end, Edwin Holmes and S. H. Pike at tackle, George “Podge” Herald and Willis Dean at guard, Arthur Goodhue at center, Amery and Lester Pool at halfback, Franklin Pike at fullback and Forrest Kenerson at quarterback. The in-season feature describes Pool as a speedy open-field runner and sure tackler and Amery as the team’s leading punter. It also highlights Melvin March and Sidney Pike competing at left tackle, Abraham Pinciss’s defense at right tackle, and Henry Bradford’s receiving and tackling at end. School authorities and most supporters favored ending the season after Woburn despite interest in postseason games.

The archive lists Saugus as Greater Lynn League champion. Beresford said during the season that the team was claiming no title at that point. The 1942 Tontoquonian later referred to a 1922 Class C championship.

seasons.seasonNote:
Charles “Buzz” Harvey’s team won the North Shore championship and placed second in the state Class C standings, according to the town report. Co-captains Stan Green and Jim Duffy led a team that recovered from a 12–0 opening loss to Medford and went unbeaten over its final ten games. The yearbook results include seven shutouts, a 3–0 win over Salem and a 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers.

A preseason clipping described Harvey’s squad as small and identified Green at end and Duffy at guard. Tackle Pitman and halfback Harrington were among the returning veterans. Back Pratt and center Riley drew attention in practice after seeing reserve duty the previous fall.

The 21–0 win over Amesbury handed the previously unbeaten team its first loss and marked the first points it had allowed. The press called Saugus a dark-horse Class C contender ahead of the Wakefield game. Later reports placed the Sachems fourth after Needham’s first loss, third entering the Swampscott game after North Quincy fell to Norwood, and second after Saugus beat Swampscott 20–0. A 40–0 win over Marblehead pulled Saugus closer to first-place New Bedford Vocational.

Saugus added a home game against Class A Salem before its Thanksgiving date with Danvers. Contemporary coverage laid out a path to first in Class C if Saugus won both games and New Bedford Vocational lost to New Bedford High. The Schoolboy Sidelights column singled out the newly booked Salem matchup as the leading game on a quiet Saturday schedule. Seating nearly derailed the game before the Saugus Park Department agreed to add about 2,000 seats, bringing estimated capacity to about 7,500. In his preview, Ernest Dalton identified Stackpole Field as the venue and pointed to the strength of Harvey and assistant Nick Morris’s line. Joseph Bucchiere kicked the decisive field goal in the 3–0 win, with Harrington holding.

Saugus closed at home with a 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers. The Sachems led 7–6 after the first quarter and scored the game’s final 31 points. Harrington scored two touchdowns, and Eddie Shipulski, Pratt, Allen and Stan Green scored one apiece. Bucchiere kicked two extra points. The win secured second place in Class C with a 6.44 rating behind undefeated New Bedford Vocational at 6.86. The final newspaper standings list Saugus with one loss and one tie in 11 games, corroborating the 9–1–1 record.

Additional sources include contributed newspaper clippings covering the preseason roster, Amesbury, weekly and final Class C standings, Salem previews, and the Danvers box score.

seasons.seasonNote:
First-year head coach Henry “Toz” Toczylowski and assistant Edward Galligan installed a new system and led Saugus to an unbeaten Class C state championship. Before the opener, Globe columnist Harold Kaese reported that Toczylowski turned down a $6,200 offer from the NFL’s Brooklyn Dodgers and honored his $2,200 agreement to coach football and teach English at Saugus High. Halfback John “Iron Mike” Harrington and tackle Dick Macdonald were co-captains. Ernest Dalton’s preseason Boston Globe report counted five returning starters, including both captains. It projected Harrington and Eddie Shipulski at halfback, Tommy Atkins at quarterback, Welcome Goss at fullback, and Art Statuto at center.

On September 12, nearly 7,000 watched the Sachems open under the lights at Stackpole Field with a 32–0 win over Chelsea. Shipulski scored on runs of 49 and 11 yards and threw a touchdown pass to Bob Nadeau. Harrington ran 18 yards for a score and threw a 35-yard touchdown pass to Tommy Atkins. Bob Connell kicked both extra points. Chelsea crossed midfield twice and never reached the Saugus 40. Saugus then shut out Woburn 13–0. Each opening win earned eight standings points, and the Globe’s weekly roundup highlighted both Harrington and Shipulski. Harrington’s touchdown in the final minute salvaged a 6–6 tie with Class A Leominster. Shipulski and Harrington broke touchdown runs of 70 and 37 yards against Gloucester in a 14–7 win. Shipulski added a 57-yard touchdown run in the 34–0 win over Amesbury.

The Sachems shut out previously unbeaten Melrose 13–0 and defeated Revere 26–0 on Monday night, November 3, at Paul Revere Stadium after rain postponed the Saturday game. Harrington and Shipulski scored two touchdowns apiece and Bob Connell kicked two extra points. Saugus led 12–0 after three quarters and scored twice in the fourth. The yearbook singled out center Art Statuto for his defensive play against both the run and the pass in the Revere shutout. In the 34–13 win over Swampscott, the yearbook credits Shipulski and Harrington with touchdown runs of 87 and 47 yards. Holbrook’s postseason account gives those runs as 88 and 55 yards. Harrington threw to Claude Collette for the only touchdown in a 6–0 win over Marblehead.

The Globe’s weekly ratings show how Saugus pulled ahead in Class C. Saugus and Winchester shared the early lead going into the Gloucester game. After the Amesbury win, Saugus had outscored its first five opponents 99–13 and was tied with Marlboro at 7.00. The win at Melrose, then the Class B leader, earned Saugus eight standings points and moved it into sole possession of first at 7.17. Saugus was idle the following weekend, and its lead grew when Marlboro tied Wellesley. The Revere win brought Saugus to 51 standings points through seven games, a 7.29 average. After the Swampscott win, Saugus led Attleboro 7.13 to 6.00 with Marblehead and Wakefield left to play.

Saugus had already clinched Class C before Thanksgiving. The win over Wakefield added eight standings points and raised Saugus’s final rating to 7.30, a figure that would have ranked third among Class A teams, behind Lynn Classical and Salem. Unbeaten, untied Attleboro finished second in Class C at 6.00, followed by Winchester and Danvers.

Shipulski led the team with 84 points entering Thanksgiving, but an elbow injury kept him out of the starting backfield. Russ Babcock started at halfback alongside Harrington. After a scoreless first half before a reported 10,000 at Stackpole Field, Welcome Goss scored from one yard in the third quarter and from three yards in the fourth. Harrington helped set up both touchdowns, and Shipulski contributed to the second drive. Wakefield’s Larry Bartnick threw a touchdown pass to Red Czarnota in the closing seconds. Saugus won 12–6. The Globe and yearbook agree on 12–6. A later rivalry table lists 13–6.

In Robert Holbrook’s postseason interview, Toczylowski credited the championship to team balance. He singled out Harrington as a triple-threat back and Shipulski as the fastest player on the squad, highlighting Shipulski’s performance against Melrose and Harrington’s late score against Leominster. He also praised Atkins’s blocking and Larry Daniels’s play at guard. Atkins lined up at quarterback while Harrington called signals.

Harrington made the Boston Globe’s All-Scholastic second team at back and its North Shore All-Scholastic eleven. Globe honorable mentions went to ends Claude Collette and Stanley Wladkowski, tackles Dick Macdonald and Doo Pendlebury, guards Larry Daniels and Lennie Flaherty, center Art Statuto, and backs Welcome Goss and Eddie Shipulski.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas, a former Boston College tackle, took over from Dave Lucey in the spring. George Laskey’s running stood out in a spring scrimmage against Lowell, and the report credited center Alan Speak and guard Dan Murphy for controlling the middle. Tom Sheehan, Mike Harrington, Alan Campbell and Andy Forti helped throughout spring practice, with Art Spinney and John Quinlan also lending a hand. Janusas installed the T formation. Gene Mack Jr. identified left end Eddie Ayers as the leading receiver, with Art Rowe and Bill Calhoun returning on the line and Frank Forti at fullback. Anganis doubled as a punter, and sophomore Sardi Nicolo pushed him for time at left halfback. Saugus was outweighed in each of its first four games and still opened 3–1. Captain Ernie Anganis, quarterback Earl Dudman and tackle Eugene Decereau gave Janusas experienced players around Laskey. Saugus played independently in 1947. The Globe reported the school’s readmission to the Northeastern Conference the following October.

Brookline won its 17th straight game in the 12–6 opener. Anganis recovered a fumble in the end zone for Saugus’s touchdown. Laskey intercepted a pass and returned it 12 yards, then had an 80-yard kickoff-return touchdown called back for clipping. His 27-yard reception helped get Saugus to the three, and the Sachems were a foot from the goal line when time expired. Janusas earned his first win the next week, 7–0 before a reported 7,000 at Beverly’s Hurd Stadium. Two Anganis completions to Ayers gained 42 yards. Laskey’s 16-yard catch and four-yard run set up Anganis’s two-yard touchdown, and Decereau kicked the extra point.

Trailing Chelsea 13–0 in the third quarter, Saugus got a spark from Laskey’s 45-yard kickoff return and 30-yard reverse. Anganis threw to Frank Forti for the first Sachem touchdown. Decereau recovered a fumble at the nine, and Laskey scored on the next play to help put Saugus ahead. Center Alan Speak intercepted a pass and returned it 28 yards to the Chelsea 19. Anganis found Ayers for 16 yards during the ensuing drive, then scored from the three, and Decereau kicked all three extra points in the 21–13 win. Against Amesbury, Laskey ran for 102 yards on 13 carries before a reported 5,000 at Stackpole Field. He caught a pass from Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and ran the final 30 yards of the 60-yard scoring play, then added an eight-yard touchdown run in the 14–6 win.

Anganis capped the opening 56-yard drive against Revere with a 24-yard touchdown run. Saugus trailed 7–6 at halftime. Dudman found Laskey for a first down and Anganis for 27 yards before Forti finished the 57-yard winning drive from the one. The 13–7 win was followed by a 14–0 shutout of Lynn English before a reported 12,000 at Manning Bowl. Saugus led 16–3 in first downs and 278–34 in rushing yards. Art Rowe recovered a fumble to start the first scoring drive, and a long Anganis run with a lateral to Forti set up the score. Saugus intercepted two passes. Dudman scored from the one on a sneak and Anganis found Laskey for a 20-yard touchdown. The win ended English’s 11-game unbeaten run, gave Saugus five straight wins and lifted the Sachems from fifth to first in the Class B ratings at 6.67.

The streak ended in a 20–7 loss to Lynn Classical before a reported 18,000 at Manning Bowl. Dan Murphy and Ed Falasca blocked a quick kick that Jim Burns recovered at the Classical 20. Anganis threw to Dudman for a touchdown, and Decereau’s kick made it 7–0. Classical tied it by halftime and added two second-half touchdowns. The Globe preview focused on cousins Ernie Anganis and Harry Agganis. Against Swampscott, Anganis left with a recurring knee injury, and Laskey scored twice on the ground in a 20–0 shutout. Dudman returned a punt 86 yards to the two and scored on the next play. With Laskey and Anganis sidelined against Marblehead, Nicolo and Fred Quinlan helped Saugus win 14–6. Ed Ayers blocked a punt, a Nicolo completion set up a Dudman sneak, and Quinlan broke a long touchdown run before halftime.

Saugus entered Thanksgiving needing a win over Peabody and losses by both Brookline and Gloucester to take Class B. Peabody led 6–0 at halftime on a one-yard run by Connors. Saugus reached the Peabody 20 in the third quarter before Laskey was injured. Art Drivas caught a deflected touchdown pass in the final minute, and Regis converted to finish the 13–0 win. The Sachems finished 7–3, fifth in Class B at 5.40, with 116 points scored, 77 allowed and three shutouts.

Laskey and Decereau made both the Boston Globe Class B All-Star team and the Lynn Item All-Scholastic team. The Boston Post also identified Laskey as one of its All-Scholastic selections. Laskey won the Thomas R. Atkins Memorial Trophy, and Decereau won the Lawrence P. Daniels Memorial Trophy. Lynn Classical’s George Bullard later called Laskey the best individual player he faced.

Dudman played in the November 29 Massachusetts All-Star team’s 40–0 win over New Hampshire. Laskey was selected for that game and did not play. On December 7 at Manning Bowl, Laskey scored on a two-yard plunge and Decereau kicked an extra point in the North Shore All-Stars’ 19–6 win over Suburban Boston before a reported 12,000. The all-star game falls outside the Saugus season statistics.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas coached the Sachems, and guard Ed Falasca captained the team. Saugus dropped its first seven games, then won three of its last four. Four losses came by seven points or fewer. The 11 documented game scores account for 117 Saugus points and 144 opponent points.

Sept. 11 at Salem, L 12–20. Nearly 8,000 saw Saugus complete seven of eight passes for 170 yards at Bertram Field. Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo found Ken Neale for a 69-yard touchdown on Saugus’ first offensive play after Salem scored. Bill Calhoun intercepted a screen pass in the third quarter, setting up a drive that Fred Quinlan finished off tackle. Calhoun’s extra-point try hit the crossbar, leaving Salem ahead 13–12 before Sam Cronis scored the clincher in the fourth.

Sept. 18 vs. Brookline, L 6–7. Saugus led 11–6 in first downs and had a 70-yard drive stopped at the Brookline four. Jim Blunt later scored on a quarterback sneak after an 18-yard Richie Nicolo pass to Neale and short runs by Frank Forti and Sardi. Paul Penda scored for Brookline with 55 seconds left, and John Sheehan kicked the winning point.

Sept. 25 vs. Beverly, L 6–20. At Bertram Field in Salem, Richie Nicolo and Quinlan helped move the ball from the Beverly 45 to the 19. Richie then hit Ted Fredericks for a fourth-down touchdown that tied the game 6–6. Beverly answered on the first snap after the kickoff, and Billy Ransom scored his second touchdown in the third quarter.

Oct. 1 at Lynn Classical, L 0–6. Don Cheever scored the only touchdown at Manning Bowl, and Jim Marano blocked the conversion. Quinlan’s 35-yard punt return helped Saugus reach the Classical nine. The Sachems lost fumbles there and later at the Classical 24.

Oct. 9 at Amesbury, L 13–27. Forti and Quinlan scored in the first half at Landry Stadium, and Hogle added a point after. Amesbury turned an interception and a blocked punt into scoring opportunities and completed six of nine passes for 103 yards.

Oct. 14. The Northeastern Conference voted in Middleton to readmit Saugus in football, baseball and basketball. The school had left the conference in 1939. The report noted that Saugus had recently been classified Class A. Amesbury and Swampscott were already on the 1948 schedule. The Chelsea preview also reported that injuries had limited the Sachems against Amesbury and that Janusas expected Sardi back.

Oct. 16 at Chelsea, L 6–25. Gene Macomber scored three times before about 3,500 at Chelsea Memorial Stadium. Les DeMasi scored from the 10 with 15 seconds left to finish a 36-yard Saugus drive. Chelsea’s victory was its first over Saugus in eight years.

Oct. 22 at Lynn English, L 0–7. Saugus reached the English 26 before halftime ran out at Manning Bowl. A fourth-quarter fumble at the Saugus 22 set up the only score, an eight-yard fourth-down pass from Bob Caulfield to Lou Tsiropoulos, who also converted.

Oct. 30 at Revere, W 20–0. Sardi, Neale and Don Junkins scored, and Hogle converted twice at Paul Revere Stadium. Saugus scored in each of the first three quarters. The brief gives the scorers without identifying how the touchdowns were made.

Nov. 6 vs. Swampscott, W 14–0. The teams were scoreless through three quarters at Stackpole Field. Sardi broke the tie with a 14-yard run to finish a 59-yard drive and later scored from the 12. Hogle added both points after.

Nov. 15 at Marblehead, L 13–19. Forti pinned Marblehead at its three with a punt and later ran 17 yards for a touchdown. Saugus led 13–12 until a late fumble at the Marblehead 35 gave the hosts the ball. Gardner Hamlen hit Dave Bartlett for a 65-yard touchdown with five seconds left. The game story attributes Saugus’ first touchdown, a two-yard run, to Quinlan, while its scoring summary credits Richie Nicolo. The individual totals leave that touchdown unassigned.

Nov. 25 vs. Peabody, W 27–13. More than 3,500 watched at Stackpole Field as Saugus set a series scoring record and posted its highest score of the season. Dan Murphy recovered a fumble at the Peabody 32, and a Charlie Woodell catch helped set up Sardi’s opening touchdown. Sardi threw two touchdown passes to Neale and a fourth-down touchdown pass to Quinlan after Andy Thain deflected it. Sardi also returned a kickoff 27 yards, Richie hit Quinlan for 28 yards, and Forti had runs of 37, 14 and 13 yards. The Item credits Fredericks and Junkins with blocking an extra point together. The Item puts Sardi’s touchdown run at three yards and describes a separate 25-yard run on the final scoring drive. The Globe reports a 19-yard touchdown run. The individual yardage uses the Item play-by-play for that game.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas coached Saugus to a 9–1 regular season and a 10–1 finish with the Exchange Bowl victory. Senior halfback Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and senior guard Dan Murphy were co-captains. The Sachems scored 281 points and allowed 54 in ten regular-season games (288–60 including the bowl). They won their final nine games and shared North Shore honors with Gloucester. Harvey L. Southward named Janusas and Gloucester’s Nate Ross his area coaches of the year.

Sept. 9 · Joyce Jamboree, Manning Bowl. Saugus beat Lawrence 13–0 in a 15-minute preseason exhibition. Richie Nicolo scored on a sneak, Sardi recovered a fumble and later scored on a 20-yard run, and Leo Kane converted. The exhibition is excluded from the standings and player statistics.

Sept. 17 · Brookline, W 26–14. The Sachems broke a two-game losing streak against Brookline on its home field. The newspaper scoring summary credits Sardi with two touchdowns and three interceptions, Richie with a 40-yard touchdown run, Charlie Woodell with a touchdown and Kane with two extra points. The yearbook also credits Woodell with a 35-yard end-around score. The two accounts describe the order and details of the Nicolo touchdowns differently.

Sept. 24 · Beverly, L 15–20. At Manning Bowl, Bill Ransom returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown. Don Banks and Leo Kane then trapped Ransom in the end zone for a safety. A 28-yard Richie Nicolo pass to Ted Frederick helped set up Sardi’s scoring run. Fred Quinlan put Saugus ahead again in the fourth quarter and Kane converted. Officials ruled a disputed pass a Beverly completion after Richie came away with the ball. Beverly regained the lead on a pass to Ransom. This was Saugus’s only loss.

Sept. 30 · Lynn Classical, W 20–7. Saugus led 14–0 at halftime at Manning Bowl. Richie’s 35-yard completion to Frederick set up Quinlan’s first short touchdown. Sardi added a rushing score, Kane kicked both first-half conversions and Quinlan scored again from the 5. The newspaper scoring summary credits Quinlan with two touchdowns and Nicolo with one. The yearbook prose gives the pair to Sardi. The newspaper split reconciles with the published season scoring totals.

Oct. 8 · Amesbury, W 27–0. At Stackpole Field, Sardi scored twice, including a 53-yard run on a reverse after Fred Flaherty intercepted a pass. Richie scored on a sneak, and Sardi’s 30-yard pass to Frederick set up Woodell’s end-around in the more detailed Amesbury report. Kane kicked three extra points. Saugus recorded 309 rushing yards and 44 passing yards as a team. The shorter newspaper account assigns different scorers. The detailed account and the season scoring totals support the two Sardi touchdowns and the Woodell score.

Oct. 15 · Chelsea, W 40–0. Saugus scored two touchdowns in each of the first three quarters at Stackpole Field. Sardi ran for three touchdowns, including a 53-yarder. Richie ran for one and threw scoring passes to Frederick and Woodell. The yearbook credits Kane with two kicks. The newspaper credits D. Murphy with a safety on Chelsea quarterback Rubenstein. The squad roster identifies him as Dan Murphy.

Oct. 21 · Lynn English, W 21–0. Before a reported 10,000 at Manning Bowl, Sardi broke the scoreless tie late in the first half with a punt-return touchdown. He added a rushing touchdown after halftime, and Richie threw a touchdown pass to Quinlan. The game report credits Frederick with catching a conversion and Sardi with running in the other two. The yearbook and newspaper differ on the yardage of the scoring plays.

Oct. 29 · Revere, W 53–0. Saugus led just 6–0 at halftime before scoring 47 points after the break. Quinlan had three touchdowns and Sardi two. Tony Serino added a 15-yard run, Woodell caught a Richie Nicolo touchdown pass, and Ken Richards recovered a fumble for the final touchdown. The yearbook identifies the 53 points as a school single-game scoring record at the time.

Nov. 5 · Swampscott, W 28–0. At Blocksidge Field, Richie scored on runs of 6 and 50 yards, Quinlan ran for touchdowns of 10 and 25 yards, and Kane kicked four extra points. Saugus completed a five-game shutout streak during which it outscored opponents 169–0.

Nov. 12 · Marblehead, W 25–7. Saugus broke a scoreless halftime tie when center Jim Marano returned an interception for a touchdown. The yearbook credits Marano with four interceptions that day. Bud DeMaci recovered a fumble before Sardi broke a 69-yard touchdown run on a triple reverse, as measured in the contemporary game account. Quinlan and DeMaci added fourth-quarter rushing scores. The Thanksgiving preview shows 26–7, but the game report and yearbook schedule agree on 25–7.

Nov. 24 · Peabody, W 26–6. Before a reported 7,500 at Stackpole Field, Richie threw two touchdowns to Woodell and Sardi ran for the other two, including one after a recovered kick. The game report and yearbook differ on the order, play lengths and extra-point attribution. Southward’s scoring recap credits Sardi with a rushing extra point and confirms that he finished the regular season with 99 points.

Dec. 3 · Exchange Bowl, Weymouth, W 7–6. Before a reported 10,000 at Manning Bowl, Saugus lost six of seven fumbles. Weymouth, previously undefeated and untied, took a 6–0 fourth-quarter lead when Bill Ahlstedt scored from the 1 after a fumble recovery. With 20 seconds left, Richie evaded the rush and threw a 50-yard touchdown pass to Sardi, who caught it near the 2 and ran it in. Frank Dudman held and Leo Kane kicked the winning extra point. Sardi also intercepted a pass earlier in the game.

Scoring and honors. Sardi led the North Shore with 16 regular-season touchdowns and three extra points (99 points), followed among Sachems by Quinlan with 10 touchdowns (60 points), Woodell with six touchdowns and a conversion (37 points), and Richie with five touchdowns (30 points). Kane led area kickers with 20 regular-season extra points. The Exchange Bowl raised Sardi to 17 touchdowns and 105 points and Kane to 21 extra points. The Boston Globe picked Sardi at back and Murphy at guard on its Class A All-Star team, separate from its overall All-Scholastic selections. The Lynn Item honored Sardi, Murphy and Quinlan.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas’s Sachems finished 8–2 and repeated as Exchange Bowl champions. They were 7–2 before the bowl and won their final seven games played. The North Shore season included one forfeit loss and one rain cancellation. Using contemporary game reports for Salem and Thanksgiving, Saugus scored 269 points and allowed 75, including the bowl and the 0–6 Beverly forfeit. Co-captains Leo Kane and Ted Frederick led a lineup that featured quarterback Richie Nicolo, halfback Jim Driscoll and end Charlie Woodell.

September 16 · Brookline, W 25–6. With Nicolo recovering from an appendectomy, Driscoll shifted to quarterback. Art Jolly finished the opening 48-yard drive. Driscoll threw two touchdowns to Woodell and completed a 17-yard pass to DeRosa before Frederick scored from the six. Dick Rumson recovered a fumble to set up Woodell’s second touchdown. Kane kicked the final extra point.

September 23 · Beverly, L 0–6 by forfeit. Beverly led 6–0 at Manning Bowl when Janusas disputed a completed pass with about three minutes left in the second quarter. Officials penalized Saugus, Janusas withdrew his team, and fighting involving players and spectators stopped play. The referee awarded the game to Beverly, and the District One headmasters’ committee later upheld the decision.

September 30 · Lynn Classical, L 6–7. Frederick scored after a 68-yard Saugus drive. An offside penalty erased Kane’s successful conversion, and Classical stopped the retry. A Saugus fumble near its own goal set up Classical’s touchdown and Joe Cottagio’s deciding extra point.

October 7 · Marblehead, W 14–6. Nicolo completed seven of eight passes. Woodell caught touchdown passes of 48 and 7 yards and added a 54-yard reception to set up the second score. Kane converted twice. Ed McIntire intercepted a pass after an early Saugus fumble, and Driscoll helped stop a Marblehead drive near the goal line.

October 14 · Chelsea, W 41–6. The yearbook credits Nicolo with touchdown runs of 21 and 11 yards and a scoring pass to Woodell. Tony Serino scored on runs of 30 and 3 yards, and Kane returned a blocked kick 33 yards for a touchdown.

October 20 · Lynn English, W 39–0. Driscoll scored from 60, 44 and 22 yards. Center Jim Marano returned an interception 27 yards for a touchdown, Charlie Murphy recovered a fumble that set up Nicolo’s one-yard score, and Kane blocked and returned a kick 10 yards for a touchdown.

October 28 · Revere, W 26–12. Saugus answered an early 12–6 deficit with two touchdown runs by Driscoll, a Nicolo sneak, and two successful conversions. Serino scored the opening touchdown. Saugus had 14 first downs and held Revere without one, with Revere losing two net yards in the second half. Nicolo and Woodell connected twice for reported gains of 17 and 31 yards.

November 4 · Swampscott, canceled. Rain washed out the game, and it was never made up.

November 11 · Salem, W 41–6. Woodell scored four times, with the yearbook identifying three of those scores as Nicolo passes. Driscoll and Jolly scored the other Saugus touchdowns and Kane kicked five extra points. The Globe’s game report and the yearbook narrative agree on 41–6. The yearbook’s schedule table prints 46–7.

November 23 · Peabody, W 47–14 at Stackpole Field. Saugus scored 27 first-quarter points and led 41–0 at halftime. Woodell scored twice. Driscoll, Jolly, Nicolo, Jack White and Charles Horman scored once each, and Kane made five of seven placements. The Globe’s same-day game account identifies both Peabody touchdowns and both extra points. The yearbook narrative gives 47–12 and its schedule table prints 47–0.

December 2 · Brockton, W 30–12 in the Exchange Bowl. Nicolo’s 23-yard completion to Woodell set up his own five-yard touchdown. After Brockton took a 12–7 lead, Nicolo found Woodell for a 38-yard score and then returned an interception 60 yards for a touchdown. His 21-yard pass to Frederick finished the scoring for Saugus, and Kane converted after all four touchdowns. Charlie Murphy and Kane helped hold Brockton to 36 rushing yards. Saugus added a late safety when Brockton recovered its blocked punt in its own end zone.

Honors and statistics. Nicolo and Driscoll made the Lynn Item All-Scholastic team. Both received Boston Globe honorable mention, along with Woodell, Kane and Murphy. Nicolo was named Exchange Bowl MVP and sat out the following day’s North Shore–Suburban All-Star game with a knee injury. Woodell led Saugus with 12 touchdowns, and Driscoll and Nicolo scored seven each. The scoring accounts identify all 40 Saugus touchdowns. Individual yardage, defensive plays and some conversion attributions are available only in part.

Bob Belyea anchored the middle, with Leahy and Doug MacNeill on the ends of the five-man front.

Oct. 10 · Saugus 12, Marblehead 12. Marblehead took a 12–0 halftime lead after long interception returns set up touchdowns. Bill MacNeill intercepted a pass for Saugus, and Belyea blocked a third-quarter punt to set up Rice’s 11-yard touchdown run. Charlie Lawrence’s completion to Donaldson opened the fourth-quarter tying drive before Whittredge carried on five straight plays and scored. Marblehead blocked the go-ahead extra-point try.

Oct. 17 · Saugus 14, Beverly 13. The teams resumed their series at neutral Bertram Field in Salem, where Saugus beat Beverly for the first time since 1947. A Bill MacNeill punt pinned Beverly at its one, and the ensuing safety proved to be the margin. The yearbook credits Leahy, Bob Randazzo and Bob Krzywicki on the play. Whittredge’s one-yard run made it 8–0 before Beverly scored twice to lead 13–8. Lawrence found Rice for a 38-yard gain on the winning 77-yard drive, which Piwowarski capped with a five-yard touchdown run in the final minute. Beverly completed a long pass on the last play and was stopped inside the Saugus 25.

Oct. 24 · Saugus 26, Lynn English 18. At Manning Bowl, Lawrence threw a 12-yard touchdown pass to Donaldson. Whittredge and Bill MacNeill scored to help build a 19–6 halftime lead. Lawrence scored the final touchdown, and Whittredge and MacNeill each converted an extra point.

Oct. 31 · Chelsea 13, Saugus 0. Tony Tiro scored both Chelsea touchdowns in the Sachems’ only regular-season defeat. Bill MacNeill’s 40-yard run was the biggest play of Saugus’s main scoring threat, which ended on downs at the Chelsea 10. The Globe singled out MacNeill and Belyea for their all-around play, and the yearbook also highlighted center Dick McAdoo.

Nov. 14 · Saugus 27, Salem 0. On Dads’ Day before 2,500 spectators, Bill MacNeill recovered a fumble and later scored from the six. Whittredge added a touchdown and Rice broke a 70-yard scoring run. Leahy recovered a fumble at the Salem 15 to set up Piwowarski’s final touchdown. The yearbook’s full game account records the shutout; a Thanksgiving preview table lists Salem with 12 points.

Nov. 26 · Saugus 33, Peabody 6. Saugus needed a win or tie to clinch the North Shore League title and led 27–0 at halftime at Leo Buckley Stadium. The newspaper box score credits Bill MacNeill and Charlie Lawrence with two touchdowns apiece and Whittredge with one. MacNeill scored from the two and broke a 50-yard crossbuck. The yearbook also describes a 50-yard Whittredge pass to Donaldson and credits Jack Lawrence and Krzywicki with touchdowns in a different scoring account. The holiday roundup confirmed the league title. Saugus finished 6–1–1 and fifth in the final Class A ratings with 62 rating points and a 7.75 average.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas entered his 13th season with a veteran backfield, a young line and little depth. He planned to build around team speed, with senior quarterback David Russell Mathews and halfbacks Jim Kelleher and Dick Burt returning. Mathews and Kelleher were co-captains. Another senior, David James Matthews, played end.

Saugus opened with a 16–14 win over Revere after trailing by 14. Janusas told Bill Shechman it was the first time in his 13 years at Saugus that his team had come back from that deficit to win. On Oct. 3, the Sachems shut out Lynn Classical 20–0 before about 4,500 fans. Ralph DeFronzo intercepted a pass to set up Kelleher’s 90-yard touchdown run. A blocked kick set up Tim Churchard’s five-yard score, and Kelleher capped a 40-yard drive with a seven-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter. Burt ran for a two-point conversion.

The yearbook records an 18–6 win over Beverly before unbeaten New Bedford handed Saugus its first loss on Oct. 10. The game was scoreless through three quarters before Stan Tenters scored twice in the fourth, the second time after New Bedford recovered a fumble at the Saugus three. A follow-up reported that quarterback Mathews was out.

Saugus beat Lynn English 44–12 on Oct. 23. Burt scored on runs of 20 and 27 yards in the first five minutes and added a third touchdown after halftime. Quarterback Mathews threw two touchdown passes to end Matthews and scored the final touchdown himself. On Oct. 31, Saugus and Swampscott played to a 0–0 tie. Saugus reached the Swampscott 20 in the first half and later stopped Swampscott on downs at the Saugus 19. The tie left the Sachems 4–1–1.

At Brookline on Nov. 14, the Sachems trailed 8–6 at halftime before Brookline scored 22 unanswered points. Mathews’s 18-yard pass to Bucchiere produced the only Saugus touchdown in the 30–6 loss. The report calls the receiver Jim Bucchiere. The yearbook identifies Francis Bucchiere as the team’s end, and the Thanksgiving report calls him Frank.

On Thanksgiving, about 8,500 fans at Stackpole Field saw Saugus defeat Peabody 14–6. Mathews found Frank Bucchiere for a first-quarter touchdown and ran in the two-point conversion. In the fourth quarter, Peabody tried a fourth-down pass from its own 20 and turned the ball over on downs. Burt finished the short drive with a one-yard touchdown run. Kelleher led the Saugus defense, which held Peabody to a late Pete Wahtera touchdown. The win denied Peabody the Class A championship after Brockton tied Weymouth 8–8. Saugus finished 6–2–1 and shared the North Shore League title with Salem.

The Lynn Item chose quarterback Mathews for its first All-Star team and Burt for its second team. The Boston Globe’s Dec. 6 “On the Bench” list recognized quarterback Mathews at back and end Matthews at end. Burt also received the school’s John A. W. Pearce Football Award.

A Paolini interception set up Maguire’s four-yard score, and Saugus led 16–0 just 3:02 into the game. Paolini added a two-yard touchdown run, and Chuck Shipulski’s fake punt produced an 81-yard touchdown pass to Serino in the 29–0 shutout. A week later, Shipulski intercepted a pass on Lynn English’s first play from scrimmage, setting up the first of Serino’s two touchdowns in a 40–0 win.

Both Saugus and Swampscott entered their Oct. 29 meeting at 5–0. Before an estimated 10,000 at Stackpole Field, Serino scored on a 12-yard rollout and found Murray for a 36-yard touchdown just before halftime. Dick Jauron scored all 13 Swampscott points, including the deciding extra point. Neither team scored in the second half, and Swampscott stopped a late Saugus drive at its 10-yard line to win 13–12.

Saugus rebounded with a 35–14 win at Winthrop. Serino ran for touchdowns of 22 and 20 yards and threw a 25-yard scoring pass to Chuck Bilton as the Sachems built a 29–0 halftime lead. Kimball and Paolini also scored on runs. Against Salem, Serino’s seven-yard pass to Paolini and Paolini’s conversion catch tied the game 8–8 before halftime. Jimmy Britton’s second touchdown with six minutes left gave Salem a 14–8 win.

On Thanksgiving at Leo Buckley Stadium, Kimball scored on runs of one and 45 yards in the first quarter, and Paolini returned the second-half kickoff 80 yards for a touchdown. Maguire, Dancewicz, Whitehurst and R. Nicolo also scored in the 48–0 win over Peabody, the team’s third shutout. The Lynn Item named six Sachems to its regional All-Star team, and the Globe gave Dancewicz and Maguire All-Scholastic honorable mentions.

Paul Maguire’s Sachems finished 7–2, winning seven games for only the second time in 19 years according to the yearbook. The senior-heavy team carried over three wins from the end of 1968, including an upset of undefeated Peabody, and opened 1969 with five more. Bill Babcock, Richard Conti and John Richard captained the team. Bob Osgood led the passing game, with Greg Manship, Mike Annese and Dan Madden among his targets. Richard and Dan Heaney powered the ground game.

Saugus opened 29–6 over B.C. High before a reported 6,000. Heaney scored on runs of 82 and 61 yards, and Richard rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns. In the 28–20 win at Beverly’s Hurd Stadium, Osgood hit Manship for 73 yards and helped turn a pass to Richard into an 80-yard touchdown when Richard lateraled to Heaney just before halftime. Osgood found Madden on fourth-and-eight and Annese for the go-ahead touchdown. Heaney sealed the win on a 40-yard run on fourth-and-three, and Richard rushed for 115 yards.

Conti supplied the only points in a 3–0 shutout at Woburn. The game recap credits him with a 44-yard field goal after an offside penalty erased his first make. A later Globe profile lists the kick at 35 yards and describes Conti’s return from a broken leg the previous season. Saugus kept Woburn from reaching midfield in the second half. Lineman John McBride broke his leg in the game. Richard helped carry the offense past Marblehead, 12–7.

Osgood completed six passes for 259 yards and three touchdowns in the 28–26 win over Newburyport. Richard scored on catches of 76 and 43 yards and a two-yard run, then caught a two-point conversion. Heaney’s 11-yard run on a fake field goal set up Richard’s rushing score. Steve Nelson made two key tackles to turn back a Newburyport drive. The Globe’s narrative credits Manship with the decisive 50-yard touchdown catch, while its scoring summary credits Madden.

Swampscott ended Saugus’s eight-game streak with a 27–6 win at Blocksidge Field for its own 24th straight victory. Richard scored from the one, Doug Waybright recovered a fumble and Osgood went 4-for-16 for 91 yards. Saugus rebounded 30–6 against Winthrop at Stackpole Field, rushing for 232 yards. Heaney and Richard each scored twice. Ed Wadleigh recovered a fumble at the Saugus one, and Osgood threw to Richard for a 99-yard touchdown two plays later. Conti kicked a field goal and three extra points.

Ron Smith and Heaney scored on runs on the first two Saugus possessions in a 29–13 win over Watertown. Osgood crossed 1,000 passing yards, threw a touchdown and two conversions to Manship, and ran for a score. At Stackpole Field on Thanksgiving, Peabody won 30–6 before a reported 10,500 to finish 9–0 and claim Class A. Osgood scored on a five-yard scramble and completed eight passes for 70 yards, bringing his season totals to 54 completions, 1,157 passing yards and eight touchdown passes. Swampscott won Class B, with Saugus seventh in the final Class B standings.

Osgood and Bill Eichel made the NEC first team on offense and Nelson made it on defense. DeSisto, Babcock, Conti and Richard received NEC honorable mention. The Lynn Item honored DeSisto and Osgood. The Boston Globe listed Osgood and Nelson on its All-Scholastic bench and Class B All-Star team, with Richard receiving honorable mention at back. Osgood was also selected as a North quarterback for the 1970 Harry Agganis All-Star game.

Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems finished 6–4 under captain Steve Spinney, scoring 158 points and allowing 118. They won five straight after losing to Gloucester and shut out Lynn English and Swampscott.

John Nicolo’s 10-yard run and Mike Burt’s two-point pass to Frank Scuzzarella gave Saugus an 8–6 win at Winthrop in its Northeastern Conference opener. Nicolo ran for both Saugus touchdowns in the 18–12 loss to Gloucester. At Marblehead, Nicolo scored from the 4 and Spinney returned an interception 39 yards for the deciding touchdown in a 12–7 win.

The Sachems scored all 20 points in the first quarter against Lynn English. Steve Desloges caught a 32-yard touchdown from Burt and ran for another score, and Nicolo added a 28-yard touchdown run. At Swampscott, Desloges broke a scoreless tie in the third quarter and Nicolo ran for two fourth-quarter touchdowns in a 19–0 win. Nicolo ran for a touchdown and returned a punt 66 yards for another in the 27–14 win over Lynn Classical. Desloges and Jim Wiswall also scored on the ground, and Spinney caught a two-point pass from Burt.

Burt threw touchdown passes to Tom Heaney and Scuzzarella in the 26–14 win at Danvers, with rushing scores from Desloges and Wiswall. Wiswall scored from the 1 in the 18–7 loss to Salem, and Burt found Scuzzarella for a 35-yard touchdown in the 20–7 loss to Beverly.

On Thanksgiving at Peabody, Desloges scored on a 1-yard run and Burt threw touchdown passes of 25 yards to Wiswall and 40 yards to Scuzzarella. Nicolo ran in a two-point conversion to help build a 20–7 halftime lead. His conversion was his only score that day. Peabody scored twice in the fourth quarter and won 21–20 on Peter Kitsakos’ two-point run.

The ten scoring summaries account for 24 Saugus touchdowns. Nicolo scored nine (eight rushing and one punt return), Desloges six (five rushing and one receiving), Wiswall four (three rushing and one receiving), and Scuzzarella three (all receiving). The Division II scoring table lists Nicolo with nine touchdowns and 54 points. The Thanksgiving box score documents two additional points on his conversion, bringing his total across the ten games to 56. Heaney caught a touchdown and Spinney scored on his interception return. Burt threw six touchdown passes, kicked eight extra points and threw two two-point conversion passes. Nigro opened the scoring at Lynn English with an 86-yard kickoff return for a touchdown in the 19–14 win.

The November 25 Boston Evening Globe reported that Saugus finished third in Division 2, behind Super Bowl qualifiers Dartmouth and Boston College High.

seasons.seasonNote:
Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems arrived at Stackpole Field for the opener having lost 34 straight games. They blanked Winthrop 25–0 behind 178 yards on 29 carries and two touchdowns from junior L.J. McKanas. John Plunkett added 71 rushing yards, and Mike Mabee threw a touchdown pass. Carlo Abate stopped Winthrop on fourth-and-one early in the game. The Item credited Saugus with 354 yards of offense and Winthrop with 116.

Plunkett ran for 169 yards and two touchdowns in a 28–8 win over Danvers. Saugus followed with a 28–14 win over Salem, its first in that matchup in 20 years, and entered the Boston Herald’s Sweet 16 at No. 16. A 20–7 win over Beverly made it 4–0. After a loss to Gloucester, Saugus beat Marblehead 47–6 and Lynn English 50–20 to reach 6–1 and secure its first winning season since 1990. At Manning Bowl against English, Mabee threw for two scores, ran for another and intercepted two passes. McKanas ran for 149 yards and three touchdowns.

Saugus dropped its last three games, including a 34–14 Thanksgiving loss to Peabody at Stackpole. Mabee returned for the finale while recovering from a broken bone in his leg. Fellow captain Matt Nazzaro, defensive tackle Dan Wass and tight end Derek Bilton also left the game with injuries. Ginolfi cited a 6–4 finish in the Item’s postgame report.

The Item’s postseason profiles credited Mabee with 61 completions for 720 yards and six touchdowns, plus 360 rushing yards, seven rushing touchdowns, six interceptions and two fumble recoveries. Abate led the team with 115 tackles and added four interceptions and four fumble recoveries. Both earned Item and Northeastern Conference recognition. McKanas was also an NEC All-Star.

history: A Brief History of Saugus High Football
Introduction

Saugus High School’s football program boasts over a century of tradition marked by unforgettable triumphs, legendary players, and the unyielding spirit of a small-town community in Massachusetts. From its humble beginnings in the early 1900s to its golden era of state championships, the Sachems have woven a rich tapestry of history that continues to inspire “Sachem Pride” to this day. This overview traces the program’s key eras, coaches, stars, and milestones, celebrating its enduring legacy despite recent challenges.
1900–1919 (The Early Years):
J.W. Stanley (1901)

The season archive’s earliest listed Saugus High team is the 1901 squad, coached by J. W. Stanley and featuring Charles “Chas” Bennett. A separate 1896 gallery clipping reports a Saugus football team without explicitly identifying it as Saugus High School. Surviving 1906 reports document a partial schedule and identify John Thomas Brady as captain. The archive resumes its regular season chronology in 1914; gaps in the surviving material should not be treated as proof that no football was played.
Arthur L. William (1914)

Saugus High has fielded a football team in most seasons since 1914. The 1914 team was coached by Arthur L. William. Saugus went 2-7 during Coach Williams’ lone season as Head Coach. The team was led by players John Fox and George Sprague.
Charles T. Senay (1915-1916)

Charles T. Senay guided Saugus High through two of the strongest early seasons preserved in the football archive. His 1915 team finished undefeated at 6–0, and the 1916 squad followed with a 7–1 record. Together, the two teams went 13–1, establishing an impressive standard for the young program. George Sprague, John Flynn, and Mike Garofano are among the players named in the surviving season records. Both teams competed in the Greater Lynn League, although no championship has yet been verified for either year. Contemporary Saugus town reports also illustrate the school's growing commitment to athletics: the 1915 report praised the football program's progress during the preceding fall, while the 1916 report described improved school spirit and the creation of an Athletic Council. These reports provide historical context rather than independent confirmation of the 1915–1916 scores or a title.
Edward Collier (1917)

The season records list Edward Collier’s 1917 team at 0–5. No coach or season record is established for 1918 in this collection. The interruption’s cause has not been verified; the wartime and influenza context alone does not establish an explanation.
1920–1950: (The Golden Years):

The period from 1920 through 1950 is widely regarded as the “Golden Era” of Saugus football. During that stretch, Saugus won state championships in 1941 and 1944 and Exchange Bowl championships in 1949 and 1950, and produced several other teams that were strong enough to be considered among the best in program history.
Fred Beresford (1920–1922, 1928)

Fred Beresford’s 1922 Warriors finished 9–0–2 behind captain Edward “Googie” Amery and fullback Franklin “Ooze” Pike. Saugus beat Danvers 24–6 on Thanksgiving and closed with a 20–9 win over Woburn. The archive lists the team as Greater Lynn League champions. The 1942 yearbook retrospectively describes a Class C title, while Beresford said during the 1922 season that he was claiming no title at that point.
William Bangs (1923–1925)

William Bangs took over in 1923 and coached through 1925. Bangs maintained competitiveness but did not produce a winning season, finishing 6–6 in his final year. Some notable players on those Bangs teams were Pool and Amery, as well as Ernest Belliveau, Homer McNutt, Wally Gautreau, and Danton Sawyer.

Albion Rice coached in 1926–1927 and returned for 1929–1934 after Fred Beresford’s 1928 season. The archive lists a 7–4 finish in 1927, a 0–9 record in 1928 and a 7–2 season in 1931. The gallery’s 1928 review highlights captain Reggie Goss, Gilman Cann, Carroll Freeman, Red Hunnewell, Stuart Kidder and Jim Foley, including a long Kidder-to-Goss pass in the Thanksgiving loss to Mission High. Its 1929 account records victories over Manchester and Swampscott, while the 1930 pages celebrate captain Jim Muzzy, also spelled Muzzey, and Laurie Templeman. The 1931 season entry names George Riley, Joe Nelson, Malcolm Bisbee, Harry Gates, Red Doherty and Joe Scarozza.
John “Jack” Leahy (1935–1936)

John “Jack” Leahy, a former Saugus captain, coached the 1935 and 1936 teams. The town report confirms seven wins in ten varsity games in 1935. Saugus closed that season with an 18–12 Thanksgiving win over Danvers. The 1936 season archive lists a 2–7–1 finish.

Throughout its history, Saugus has primarily been known as the Sachems, a nickname that began during the Leahy era. Prior to the Sachems nickname and mascot, Saugus used other nicknames including Warriors (1914–1929) and Eagles (1930–1934).
Charles “Buzz” Harvey (1937–1940)

Charles “Buzz” Harvey coached Saugus from 1937 through 1940. His 1939 team finished 9–1–1 and won the North Shore championship, as recalled in the 1942 yearbook and corroborated by the contemporary town report. Co-captains Jimmy Duffy and Stan Green led a team featuring John “Iron Mike” Harrington, Art Statuto, Eddie Shipulski and their teammates. The gallery recounts the 3–0 victory over Salem and the 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers, followed by a celebratory trip to New York and West Point. The town report places Saugus second in Class C; this regional championship should not be described as a verified 1939 state title.

Championship spotlight — 1939: Charles “Buzz” Harvey and assistant Nicholas Morris built a North Shore championship team whose success attracted statewide attention. After an opening loss to Medford, Saugus went unbeaten the rest of the season, including a tie with powerful Melrose and a memorable 3–0 victory over Salem. Weekly newspaper reports tracked Saugus climbing from fourth to second in Class C. After beating Marblehead, the Sachems added a home game against Class A Salem, giving them a chance to finish first if they also beat Danvers and New Bedford Vocational lost to New Bedford High. The 1939 school report credited Saugus as the second-highest-scoring team in Massachusetts and second in the Class C standings among 51 teams. The School Committee celebrated the achievement with a five-day educational trip to New York City.
Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski (1941–1942)

Boston College graduate Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski succeeded Harvey in 1941 after the NFL’s Brooklyn Dodgers selected him 78th overall. Toczylowski captained Frank Leahy’s 1940 Boston College team, which finished 11–0 and beat Tennessee in the Sugar Bowl. Charlie O’Rourke quarterbacked that team. The New York Sun selected Toczylowski for its 1940 first-team All-America backfield.

Toczylowski and assistant Edward Galligan guided Saugus to the 1941 Class C state championship. Co-captains John “Iron Mike” Harrington and Dick Macdonald led a team that included Eddie Shipulski, Art Statuto and Eddie Koschei. Harrington earned Boston Globe All-Scholastic second-team and North Shore All-Scholastic recognition. The 1942 Saugus town report records a 7–3–1 season in Toczylowski’s second year. He later entered the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame.

Championship spotlight — 1941: The 1941 Sachems won the Massachusetts Class C state championship and finished unbeaten. A contemporary Boston Globe retrospective gives 10–0–1. The yearbook schedule and final Class C standings document ten games, and the nine wins and one tie in the surviving results account for all ten. Superintendent Vernon W. Evans recognized coaches Henry Toczylowski and Edward Galligan in the town report.
Dave Lucey (1943–1946)

Dave Lucey succeeded Toczylowski in 1943 and coached through 1946. His 1944 team went 10–0 in the regular season and won the Massachusetts Class B championship. Captain Art Spinney earned Boston Globe All-Scholastic first-team honors at end. Spinney later started four seasons at Boston College, captained the 1949 Eagles and entered the Boston College Varsity Club Athletic Hall of Fame in 1972. He played for the Baltimore Colts in 1950 and again from 1953 to 1960 after Army service. He earned Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition in the 1959 and 1960 seasons and helped Baltimore win NFL championships in 1958 and 1959. Doug Waybright captained Saugus in 1943, graduated in 1944 and earned his first Notre Dame football letter that fall. He returned after Army service and was on Notre Dame’s 1947 and 1949 championship teams. Saugus later named an elementary school in his memory.

Championship spotlight — 1944: Under Dave Lucey, the 1944 Sachems ran through ten regular-season games without a loss to earn the Massachusetts Class B championship. The archive records a dominant 207 points scored and only 19 allowed during that championship run. Art Spinney, Dick Allen, Bob Kane, Don Reiniger, Frank Pyszko and Bruce Waybright were among its standouts. The yearbook also documents a separate 19–7 postseason loss to Class A champion Peabody, which does not erase the team's Class B title. The 1944 town report remembered 1939, 1941 and 1944 as three defining championship seasons.
1947–1960: (The Janusas Era):
John Janusas (1947–1960)
John Janusas coached Saugus from 1947 through 1960. His teams won consecutive Exchange Bowls in 1949 and 1950, won the North Shore League title in 1953 and shared the league title with Salem in 1959.

John Janusas’s first team went 7–3 in 1947. Captain Ernie Anganis played in a backfield that included George Laskey and Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo. Laskey earned Lynn Item and Boston Post All-Scholastic recognition and made the Globe’s Class B All-Star team. He scored for the North Shore All-Stars in their 19–6 win over Suburban Boston. Saugus finished 3–8 in 1948.

The 1949 Sachems finished 10–1, sharing the North Shore championship with Gloucester and winning the Exchange Bowl against Weymouth, 7–6. Richie Nicolo’s 50-yard touchdown pass to his brother Sal “Sardi” Nicolo tied the bowl game, and Leo Kane’s extra point secured the victory. Co-captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy led a team also featuring Fred Quinlan and Richie Nicolo. Southward’s newspaper season wrap-up credits Sardi with an area-leading 99 points and 16 touchdowns and identifies Gloucester as Class B state champion. The ten regular-season results add up to 281 points for Saugus and 54 against, matching Southward’s 281-point scoring tally. The Exchange Bowl brought the totals to 288–60. Sardi later played at LSU and scored on a 94-yard run against Rice on October 4, 1952.

Championship spotlight — 1949: John Janusas's 1949 Sachems went 10–1, shared the North Shore championship with Gloucester and won the Exchange Bowl in unforgettable fashion. Against Weymouth, Richie Nicolo connected with his brother Sal “Sardi” Nicolo on a 50-yard touchdown pass, and Leo Kane's extra point secured a 7–6 victory. Captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy helped lead a squad that brought enormous pride to Saugus. The superintendent's 1949 report singled out the Weymouth victory as a lasting community memory. This was an Exchange Bowl championship and North Shore co-title, not a documented Saugus state championship.

Championship spotlight — 1950: John Janusas’s Sachems won their second consecutive Exchange Bowl, beating Brockton 30–12 on December 2 at Manning Bowl and finishing 8–2. Richie Nicolo ran for a touchdown, returned an interception 60 yards for another and threw touchdown passes to Charlie Woodell and Ted Frederick. Co-captain Leo Kane kicked four extra points and helped Charlie Murphy anchor the line that held Brockton to 36 rushing yards. Woodell led Saugus with 12 touchdowns across the season.

The 1953 North Shore League champions finished 6–1–1 in regular-season play; the yearbook lists the Joyce Jamboree loss separately. Co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill led the team, which clinched the title by beating Peabody 33–6 on Thanksgiving. The 1954 team followed with a 6–3 season under co-captains Jack Lawrence and Malcolm “Mal” Rice. The 1959 season records list a 6–2–1 finish and leading players David Matthews, Richie Burt and Jim Kelleher. The 1959 team is listed as North Shore League Champions, with the source qualification described in Championship Seasons.

Championship spotlight — 1953: John Janusas guided the 1953 Sachems to a 6–1–1 regular-season record and the North Shore League championship. Co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill led the way, and a commanding 33–6 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody clinched the league crown. The 1954 yearbook explicitly connects that holiday victory to the championship and records the separate Joyce Jamboree loss outside the regular-season total. It was a fitting culmination to another strong season under Janusas.

Championship spotlight — 1959: John Janusas’s Sachems finished 6–2–1 and shared the North Shore League title with Salem, as confirmed by the contemporary School Champions roundup. Co-captains Dave Mathews and Jim Kelleher led a squad that beat Peabody 14–6 on Thanksgiving and ended its Class A title bid.
1961–1972 (Sustaining Competitiveness):
Bernard Stead (1961-1963)

Bernard Stead coached from 1961 through 1963. The season archive records finishes of 0–8, 1–8 and 0–9, respectively, a combined 1–25. Tom Carr is among the notable players listed for that period; the collection does not establish that he was its only All-Star.
Walter Sheridan (1964-1966)

Walter Sheridan coached from 1964 through 1966, culminating in a 7–2 season. The gallery’s 1967 yearbook pages identify the fall 1966 co-captains as Edward Maguire, John Dancewicz and Paul Uga, alongside Christie Serino, James Mancuso, Donald Murray, Richard Lombardo and their teammates. Four pages preserve the squad portrait, named player studies, game photographs, pep squad and cheerleaders. Serino later pursued a distinguished hockey coaching career, described in his alumni profile.
Paul Maguire (1967-1972)

Paul Maguire coached from 1967 through 1972. His 1969 Sachems finished 7–2 under captains John Richard, Richard Conti and William Babcock. The yearbook names Bob Osgood and Bill Eichel to the first offensive Northeastern Conference All-Star team and Steve Nelson to the first defensive team, with honorable mentions for Rich Desisto, Babcock, Conti and Richard. The only losses came against Class B champion Swampscott and Class A champion Peabody.
1973–1983: (The Ginolfi Era):
Mike Ginolfi (First tenure 1973-1983)
Mike “Gino” Ginolfi took over as the Sachems head coach in 1973. Coach Ginolfi restored Saugus as a competitive force.

The 1975 Sachems finished 9–1 and shared the Northeastern Conference championship. Captains Tom Heaney, Doug Mackie, John Nicolo and Steve Gannon led the team. The gallery preserves the 15–14 comeback against Salem and the muddy 6–0 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody. The 1978 yearbook’s review explicitly distinguishes the shared first-place finish in 1975 from the conference title won in 1977.

Championship spotlight — 1975: Mike “Gino” Ginolfi's 1975 Sachems delivered a 9–1 season and a share of first place in the Northeastern Conference. Captains Tom Heaney, Doug Mackie, John Nicolo and Steve Gannon helped drive the resurgence. Among the season's memorable moments were a 15–14 comeback against Salem and a hard-fought 6–0 Thanksgiving win over Peabody. Later yearbook coverage and local historical reporting both recall the shared conference finish, while the school district included the team in its championship-banner recognition.
Gannon went on to play college football at Holy Cross, being one of the program’s greatest players of all time. He is a member of both the Saugus High and Holy Cross Athletic Halls of Fame.

Doug Mackie earned high-school All-American recognition in 1975 and continued his football career at Ohio State. He later played in the USFL for the Tampa Bay Bandits and New Jersey Generals and appeared in the NFL for Atlanta. His alumni profile records additional time with the Giants and Saints. The gallery and alumni collection preserve his professional career; claims that he was the nation’s top recruit or that combine his 1984 All-Pro honor with Herschel Walker’s later rushing-record season require separate documentation.

John Nicolo helped Ithaca College win the 1979 NCAA Division III football title and the 1980 Division III baseball title. He was a second-team football All-American and the 1980 Division III World Series MVP. He played for the Auburn Americans in the New York–Penn League in 1980. Ithaca inducted him individually in 1986 and later honored both championship teams. Saugus High’s inaugural 1987 Athletic Hall of Fame class included eight football alumni: Art Spinney, Christie Serino, Doug Mackie, George Laskey, John “Iron Mike” Harrington, John Nicolo, Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and Stan Green. The school roster recognizes Dr. John Mangini as an original committee member.

The Sachems followed a 2–8 season in 1976 with a 9–1 Northeastern Conference championship in 1977. The yearbook identifies co-captains Dan Hashem and Frank Doyle and senior contributors including George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, John Coffey and Tim Fawcett. A 12–10 Thanksgiving win over Peabody closed the season. The gallery also preserves Mike Ginolfi’s 1977 Item Coach of the Year recognition.

Championship spotlight — 1977: Two years after sharing the conference crown, Mike Ginolfi's 1977 Sachems won the Northeastern Conference outright with a 9–1 record. Captains Dan Hashem and Frank Doyle led a talented squad that included George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, John Coffey and Tim Fawcett. A 12–10 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody provided a memorable finish. The Sachems placed third in Division 2, with Dartmouth and Boston College High qualifying for the Super Bowl. The gallery preserves Ginolfi's 1977 Lynn Item Coach of the Year recognition. Contemporary yearbook material and later local reporting distinguish this outright title from the 1975 co-championship.

Saugus finished 6–3–1 in 1978 and 5–5 in both 1979 and 1980. The 1978 yearbook identifies returning starters Paul Nigro, Don Trainor, Bill Peach and Mike Allen. Steve Peach became a three-time Lynn Item All-Star and later played at Syracuse and Boston College, where he also punted. The gallery’s 1980 review recalls a 40–6 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody. These season summaries should be distinguished from individual alumni achievements.

The 1981 Sachems season was the worst season for Ginolfi during his first tenure as they went 1-9. Saugus bounced back in 1982 going 5-4-1. That season Saugus was led by Steve Fauci, Anthony Cogliano, Mark Strange, and Anthony Guthro. 1983 Saugus fell back to below .500 going 4-6. The team was led by Tom Trainor, Kevin Pelley, and Bob Cinelli.

Ginolfi would step down after the 1983 season and moved into athletic administration. His coaching tree shaped Saugus football for decades through assistants and former players who followed him into the head coaching role.
1984–1993: Inconsistency and Brief Success
Kevin Ward (1984-1990)

Kevin Ward took over in 1984, and the program went through several down years, though the 1987 team rebounded to go 7-3. Marc Fauci emerged as one of the Sachems greatest players. He was named Boston Globe All Scholastic in 1989. Fauci would go on to play college football at Boston University (BU). While at BU, Fauci would play Linebacker and was twice named Co-Captain as a junior and senior. Fauci led BU to arguably its best season ever in 1993 when they went 12-1 and finished the regular season with a perfect 11-0 mark, the first unbeaten and untied record in program history. Fauci was named a second-team All-America by The Sports Network and National Weekly Football Gazette and a third-team All-America selection by the Associated Press.
Mike “Bonty” Bontempo (1991-1993)

The 1990 team went 8-2, which was Saugus’s best record in years. After that, Mike “Bonty” Bontempo took over and coached through 1993, but the program struggled during that span going 1-29. During his tenure he coached All Stars Sean Publicover and Joe Attubato.
1994–2004: Rebuilding and Setbacks
Mike Ginolfi (Second Tenure 1994-1995)

Mike Ginolfi returned in 1994. After an 0–10 season, the 1995 Sachems snapped a 34-game losing streak with a 25–0 victory over Winthrop and finished 6–5, their first winning season since 1990. Co-captain Mike Mabee, a multi-sport standout, led the team with L.J. McKanas, Carlo Abate, Matt Nazzaro and Derek Bilton. The gallery preserves the streak-ending game and the 50–20 win over Lynn English that clinched a winning season. An early-season Boston Herald clipping ranked Saugus No. 16; that was not a final-season ranking.

Coach Ginolfi retired from coaching after the 1995 season. He will always be remembered as one of the greatest football coaches in Sachem history, as he was a 1993 Saugus High Athletic Hall of Fame inductee, but he was also one of the greatest coaches in Massachusetts Football History as he was inducted into the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame in 1992. Coach Ginolfi would remain Athletic Director at Saugus until he retired from that position in 2002
John Fauci (1996-1998)

John Fauci took over for Coach Ginolfi for the 1996 season. Saugus finished the 1996 season with a 4–7 record. The Sachems were led by John Plunkett, Justin Falite, and LJ McKanas. McKanas would be named to numerous All-Star teams as a RB. He would go on to play college football at Northeastern. While at Northeastern McKanas would go on to set numerous rushing records. During his Senior season in 2001 McKanas set records for most carries, 342, rushing yards, 1756, and rushing touchdowns, 14. He gained over 100 yards rushing in nine games and over 200 in three. He averaged 5.1 yards per carry and 159.6 per game as the team posted a 5-6 record. His 242 rushing yards against Massachusetts is second in the Husky record books. He won numerous awards, including All-New England, All-Conference and first-team Hanson All-America. He also received the Harry Agganis Award as the Outstanding Senior Football Player in New England. In 2009 he was inducted into the Northeastern Athletic Hall of Fame. McKanas later was a contestant on the popular TV Show Survivor. His alumni profile records a ninth-place finish. He was the first of two former Sachems to become a contestant on the popular reality show.

Saugus finished 6–4–1 in 1997 and 5–6 in 1998. The 1998 Thanksgiving preview credits Raphael Zammit with 21 total touchdowns before the finale—18 rushing, two receiving and one interception return—surpassing the previous total-touchdown mark of 20 credited to L.J. McKanas. That total-touchdown distinction should not be confused with a rushing-touchdown record. The same preview highlights quarterback Ryan Lahey (Leahy in the season workbook), Mike Panzini and their teammates; its figures are pre-Thanksgiving totals rather than confirmed final-season statistics.
Dean Sacca (1999-2000)

Dean Sacca became head coach in 1999. The 1999 season had a promising start as Saugus started the year 3-3 however Saugus would end the year 3-8. All Star George Lowe, who played almost every skilled position that year, led the team along with Brian Mirasolo. The Sachems continued to struggle in the 2000 season by going 2-8. Coach Sacca stepped down at the end of the season. Ryan Gould was the only All-Star from the 2000 team.
John Nicolo (2001-2004)

John Nicolo took over as the Sachems Head Coach in 2001. Unfortunately, Coach Nicolo’s tenure did not produce the same success as he had during his playing days. The 2001 Sachems went 2-9 and were led by Pat Quinlan, Patrick Eaton, and Kyle Sucharewicz. The 2002 Sachems went 1-10 and were led by Sal Nicolo and All-Star Anthony Barbanti. Sal Nicolo would go on to play two seasons of college football for Division III Bridgewater State Bears under Peter Mazzaferro.

The 2003 Sachems finished 3–8. Junior running back Mike Nicolo rushed for 1,462 yards and 11 touchdowns and set the then Saugus single-game rushing record with 306 yards against Salem, as documented in the gallery and alumni profile. Anthony “Beave” Barbanti’s senior profile records 75 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and three sacks, alongside his work on the offensive line. Mark Spadafora and Chris Benson also feature in the season entry.

The 2004 Sachems were plagued with injuries to their core players and the promising rebuild came to a stop as they finished the season 0-11. Nicolo missed part of the season and played most of the season with an injured knee and shoulder. Despite the injuries Nicolo was still named an All-Star along with teammate Brian Bianchi. Mike Nicolo would go on to play College Football for New England Division III power Curry College however injuries followed him throughout his college career. Nicolo was inducted into the Curry College Athletic Hall of Fame as a member of the 2007 Curry Football Team, which was ranked 19th Nationally and had won 4-consecutive New England Football Conference Championships.
After the 2004 season, Coach Nicolo stepped down as Head Coach and took on the role of Athletic Director.
2005–2016: (The Broderick Era)
Mike Broderick (2005-2016)

Mike Broderick took over in 2005 and brought stability back to the program. Coach Broderick was the first Sachems Head Coach to have not been under the Ginolfi Coaching Tree since the Paul Maguire days.

Coach Broderick’s first two seasons were rebuilding seasons for the Sachems. His 2005 team went 1-10, led by All Star Alex Klimarchuk. In 2006 the Sachems improved to 3-7. Although the record didn’t seem like much, this team was remembered for becoming the first Saugus team to defeat the Sachems Thanksgiving Day rival, the Peabody Tanners, for the first time in 18 seasons. That Sachems team was led by senior All Star, Rodney Lavoie, who went on to be a contestant on the TV Show Survivor in 2015, the second former Sachem to appear on the hit TV Show. Saugus also had a freshman QB by the name of Mike DiChiaria who had a breakout season. DiChiaria would transfer to the prep school BB&N to finish out his High School career, where DiChiaria made the top 10 in Massachusetts state history for career touchdown passes. He would go on to play college football at Cornell.

In 2007 Saugus took a major step forward and had their first winning season since 1997, going 7-3. The 2007 team was led by Paul Sullivan and All Stars Tyler Trainor, Mike Dean, and Brett Reid. The 2008 team also went 7-3 and were again led by All Stars Mike Dean and Brett Reid.

From 2009 through 2011, the Sachems fell back to below .500. Although these teams didn’t have as much success, they still had some All-Star players like Shamir Guillaume and AJ Guthro. Guillaume would go on to set the Sachems single season rushing yards record by rushing for 1,678 yards in 2010.

The Sachems finished 6–5 in 2012 and 3–8 in 2013. Tom Trainor, C.J. Randolph, Nick Benoit and Ismael Minaya are listed for 2012. Justin Winn earned Lynn Item All-Scholastic honors as a junior in 2013, when his newspaper profile credited him with 1,103 rushing yards and 19 touchdowns.

In 2014, Saugus finished 6–5. Dan Cacciola’s 375-yard, four-touchdown game against Winthrop surpassed Mike Nicolo’s earlier 306-yard single-game mark. The statistics table records 1,467 rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns for Cacciola, and 1,255 yards and 22 rushing touchdowns for Justin Winn. The archive describes Winn’s 22 rushing touchdowns as a school record. Cacciola’s surname appears as Cicciola in parts of the supplied workbook; the gallery and statistics section use Cacciola.

Saugus finished 3–9–1 in 2015 and 1–10 in 2016, as listed in the season archive. Brendan Grocki and Cam Williamson appear among the notable players for those teams. Mike Broderick’s tenure ended after the 2016 season, concluding twelve seasons as head coach.
2017 onward: Nalen, Mabee, Cummings and Bluestein
Anthony Nalen (2017)

Anthony Nalen was hired in 2017, and Saugus improved from the previous season. Ricky Martinez helped lead the Sachems. Unfortunately, due to a controversy during the 2018 off-season, Nalen was removed as head coach.
Mike Mabee (2018)

After Nalen’s departure, former Sachems great and former player under Coach Ginolfi, Mike Mabee, was hired to serve as interim Head Coach. Coach Mabee was able to guide a competitive team to a 4-7 record. The team was led by All-Star Dante McGrane.
Steve Cummings (2019–2025)

The Sachems under Coach Cummings have seen their ups and downs. The Sachems took a step back during the 2019 season when they went 3-8. The team was led by All Star Marvens Jean as well as Kyle Surette, Sal Franco, Christian Correa, and Javier Martinez.
The 2020 Season was interrupted by the Covid-19 Pandemic, but Saugus was still able to play a 7 game schedule during the season, going 2-5.
Saugus finished 0–11 in 2021 and 2–11 in 2022. Mike MacEacheran and Braden Faiella were among the players from those seasons.

The 2023 Sachems finished 5–6. Braden Faiella, Tommy DeSimmone and Dylan Clark are listed among the season’s leading players. The gallery’s senior Faiella profile reports 140 tackles and a career total of 482, and credits him with Item Defensive Player of the Year recognition. The coach’s suggestion that the career total might be a state record is not treated as a verified record. Faiella later continued his football career at Saint Anselm; the supplied workbook also spells his first name Brandon.
The 2024 Sachems went 3-8 and were led by All Stars Koby Jette and Cody Munafo.
Saugus finished 2–9 in 2025, with wins over Lynn Vo-Tech and East Boston. The Sachems closed the season with a 28–26 Thanksgiving loss at Peabody in Steve Cummings’s final year as head coach.
Greg Bluestein (2026–present)
Saugus High named alumnus and former assistant Greg Bluestein head football coach in February 2026, succeeding Steve Cummings after seven seasons.
Conclusion

Saugus football has a proud and deeply rooted history. While the program has not reached the heights of its golden era in recent times, it has produced championship caliber teams, conference titles, and many memorable players who excelled at the college and professional levels. More than wins and losses, being a Sachem has always meant pride, tradition, and commitment to the red and white.
